facts: It is the largest and oldest inhabited castle in the world, continuously occupied for over 900 years.
The station sits almost directly opposite the castle's Henry VIII Gate on the High Street.
The station building was substantially rebuilt in 1897 for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, including a private royal waiting room.
The gallery opened in 1993 on the site of a former gasworks overlooking Porthmeor Beach.
It celebrates the modern artists' colony that grew up in St Ives from the 1920s onwards, including Barbara Hepworth.
St Ives station sits directly above the beach it overlooks, with one of the most scenic approaches on the whole GWR network.
Completed in 1910, it was the first Anglican cathedral built in England since St Paul's in the 17th century.
Its three spires make it a landmark visible across much of the city.
Truro is Cornwall's only city and its county town.
Its giant biomes were built inside a disused china clay pit near St Austell.
The Rainforest Biome is the largest indoor rainforest in the world.
A connecting bus service runs from Par and St Austell stations to the site.

landmark: Bath area GWR heritage (Brunel's Great Western Main Line)
facts: Chippenham sits on Isambard Kingdom Brunel's original Great Western Main Line, opened throughout in 1841.
The line's broad-gauge origins shaped the sweeping curves still used by trains through the town today.
Chippenham was historically a key junction for routes towards Bath, Bristol, and the West Country.
Longleat was the first stately home in England to open a safari park, in 1966.
The house itself is a leading example of Elizabethan architecture, completed in 1580.
It remains the family seat of the Marquess of Bath.
Maidenhead Railway Bridge, just outside the station, has the widest, flattest brick arches ever built when Brunel completed it in 1838.
The bridge inspired J.M.W. Turner's painting 'Rain, Steam and Speed'.
Maidenhead sits on the River Thames, a popular boating town since Victorian times.
Cheltenham Racecourse hosts the Cheltenham Festival every March, considered the highlight of the National Hunt racing calendar.
Cheltenham Spa station takes its name from the town's Regency-era spa heritage, when it grew as a fashionable resort around its mineral springs.
The town's wide Regency terraces were built to attract visitors taking the waters in the early 19th century.
Slough Trading Estate, opened in the 1920s, was one of the first purpose-built industrial estates in the world.
Astronomer William Herschel, who discovered Uranus, lived and worked in Slough; Herschel Park is named after him.
Slough is a key junction for GWR services, where the short branch line to Windsor & Eton Central begins.
Reading Abbey was founded in 1121 by Henry I, who is buried on the site.
It was once one of the largest and wealthiest monasteries in England before its dissolution in 1539.
Reading station is one of the busiest interchange stations outside London, serving as a hub for GWR's western routes.
The current train shed was designed by Brunel himself and opened in 1854.
Paddington is the London terminus of the old Great Western Railway, Brunel's original broad-gauge main line.
A bronze statue of Brunel stands on the station concourse, and the Paddington Bear statue is another popular landmark there.
Powderham Castle has been the seat of the Courtenay family, Earls of Devon, since the 14th century.
It sits on the west bank of the Exe Estuary, visible from trains on the Exeter to Newton Abbot sea wall line.
Starcross was also the site of one of Brunel's experimental atmospheric railway pumping stations in the 1840s.
The railway runs directly along the sea wall through Dawlish, with waves sometimes breaking over passing trains in storms.
The line was originally built by Brunel in the 1840s as part of the South Devon Railway.
A major storm in February 2014 destroyed a section of the sea wall here, closing the line for two months.
Totnes Castle is a Norman motte-and-bailey fortress overlooking the town.
Totnes is one of England's oldest chartered towns, with a market granted in the 10th century.
The town is known today for its alternative and independent culture alongside its medieval High Street.
Exeter Cathedral has the longest uninterrupted medieval vaulted ceiling in the world.
Exeter Central is closer to the cathedral and city centre than the larger Exeter St Davids station.
The cathedral's twin Norman towers date from around 1130, older than most of the rest of the building.
Smeaton's Tower is a former lighthouse, relocated to the Hoe in the 1880s after being replaced on its offshore reef.
Sir Francis Drake is said to have finished a game of bowls on the Hoe before facing the Spanish Armada in 1588.
The Mayflower departed from Plymouth in 1620, and the city marks this with waterfront memorials near the Hoe.
Bodmin Jail opened in 1779 and was one of the first British prisons to hold prisoners in individual cells.
It is now a visitor attraction and hotel, reached by a short bus or taxi ride from Bodmin Parkway station.
Bodmin Parkway itself, despite the name, is several miles from Bodmin town centre.
Looe is a working fishing harbour split either side of the River Looe, joined by a Victorian bridge.
The Looe Valley Line branch to Liskeard is one of the most scenic short branch lines in Cornwall.
Looe holds an annual National Sea Angling Festival, reflecting its long fishing heritage.

landmark: St Erth & the St Ives Bay Line
facts: St Erth is the junction station where the branch line to St Ives leaves the Cornish Main Line.
The St Ives Bay branch is considered one of the most scenic short rail journeys in Britain, hugging the coast for its final approach.
The line was built in 1877 partly to relieve St Ives' congested streets of horse-drawn traffic to the harbour.
Fistral Beach is regarded as the birthplace of British surfing and hosts major surfing competitions.
Newquay's rail branch from Par was originally built in the 1870s to carry china clay to the harbour, only later becoming a passenger holiday line.
Newquay station still sees dedicated seasonal Sunday services from London during summer.
The Tor is topped by the roofless St Michael's Tower, the remains of a 14th-century church.
Castle Cary is the standard rail-and-bus interchange point for Glastonbury, including for the Glastonbury Festival site at nearby Pilton.
Glastonbury itself has never had its own railway station.
The 14th-century tithe barn is one of the largest and best-preserved in England.
The town also has a rare Saxon church, St Laurence's, believed to date from around 1000 AD.
Bradford-on-Avon sits on the Kennet and Avon Canal as well as the railway.
The centre preserves Great Western Railway locomotives, carriages and a working steam depot.
It sits immediately next to Didcot Parkway station, on the original GWR main line.
It includes a reconstruction of Brunel's broad-gauge railway, which used a wider track than today's standard gauge.
The regatta has been held on the Thames at Henley since 1839.
Henley-on-Thames station is the terminus of a short branch line from Twyford.
The regatta course is a straight 1 mile 550 yard stretch of the river.
Cliveden was the country home of the Astor family and a noted political and social hub in the early 20th century.
Its gardens and estate are now owned by the National Trust.
Taplow station also sits close to Cliveden Reach, a well-known stretch of the Thames for rowing.
The bridge, completed in 1832, was designed by William Tierney Clark, who later built the Chain Bridge in Budapest on a similar design.
Marlow station is the terminus of a short branch line from Maidenhead known locally as the 'Marlow Donkey'.
The bridge crosses the Thames right beside Marlow's parish church.
The gallery displays work by painter Stanley Spencer, who was born and lived in Cookham.
Spencer set many of his most famous paintings in and around the village.
Cookham sits on the Thames between Maidenhead and Marlow.

landmark: The Wind in the Willows' riverbank
facts: Author Kenneth Grahame lived at Church Cottage in Pangbourne and is buried in the village churchyard.
The stretch of the Thames around Pangbourne is often linked to the riverbank setting of The Wind in the Willows.
Pangbourne is also known for the Pang Valley, where the River Pang meets the Thames.
Pinewood Studios has been used for major film franchises including James Bond and Star Wars.
The studio complex opened in 1936 in a converted country house, Heatherden Hall.
Iver station is the nearest railhead, with the studio a short drive away.
The Vale of Evesham has been a major fruit and market-gardening area since medieval times, when Evesham Abbey monks developed its orchards.
Evesham's bell tower is one of the few remaining parts of its once-great abbey, largely destroyed at the Dissolution.
The town sits on a large bend of the River Avon.
Pershore Abbey was a Benedictine monastery; its surviving tower and choir are still used as the parish church today.
Much of the original abbey nave was demolished after the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
Pershore is also known, like nearby Evesham, for fruit growing in the Vale of Evesham.
Cirencester was the second-largest town in Roman Britain, and the Corinium Museum holds one of the country's best Roman mosaic collections.
Kemble station, on the edge of the Cotswolds, is the nearest railhead to Cirencester, which has no station of its own.
Cirencester is often nicknamed the 'Capital of the Cotswolds'.
Stroud grew rich on the wool and cloth trade, and its five valleys are still lined with former mill buildings.
The Museum in the Park is housed in an 18th-century wool merchant's mansion.
Stroud is known today for its independent shops and one of the largest farmers' markets in the country.
Gloucester Cathedral's cloisters, with their fan vaulting, were used as filming locations for the Harry Potter films.
It is the burial place of King Edward II, murdered at nearby Berkeley Castle in 1327.
The cathedral's central tower rises 68 metres above the city.
Tewkesbury Abbey has one of the largest surviving Norman crossing towers in England.
The town was the site of a decisive Wars of the Roses battle in 1471.
Ashchurch for Tewkesbury station sits a couple of miles outside the historic town centre.
STEAM is housed in a former Great Western Railway works building where locomotives were built and maintained.
Swindon grew from a small market town into a major railway town after the GWR chose it as its main works site in 1841.
The former GWR railway village of terraced housing still stands close to the station.

landmark: Salisbury Plain edge & Westbury White Horse
facts: The Westbury White Horse, cut into the chalk hillside above the town, is thought to be Wiltshire's oldest surviving hill figure.
Westbury sits on the edge of Salisbury Plain, a major military training area.
Westbury is an important railway junction where lines to Bristol, Weymouth and Salisbury diverge.
Frome's Cheap Street, with its central stone-flagged water channel, is one of England's best-preserved medieval streets.
The town was once a major centre of the wool trade, rivalling Bath in size during the 17th century.
Frome today is known for its independent shops and monthly Sunday market.
Yeovil has a long history of aircraft manufacturing, particularly with Westland Helicopters.
Yeovil Pen Mill is one of two stations serving the town, on the line between Weymouth and Bristol.
The nearby Fleet Air Arm Museum, a short drive from Yeovil, holds one of Europe's largest naval aviation collections.
Okehampton sits on the northern edge of Dartmoor, England's largest area of open moorland in the south.
The town's Norman castle ruins are the largest in Devon.
The railway line to Okehampton was reopened to regular year-round passenger services in 2021 after decades of Sunday-only running.
Ivybridge sits at the southern start of the Two Moors Way, a long-distance path running to Dartmoor and beyond.
The town takes its name from a medieval packhorse bridge over the River Erme.
Ivybridge station reopened in 1994 after the original station had closed decades earlier.
Exmouth was one of the first seaside resorts to develop in England, from the 18th century onwards.
It sits at the mouth of the River Exe, marking the start of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site.
Exmouth is the terminus of a branch line from Exeter that runs along the Exe Estuary.
Barnstaple is the terminus of the 'Tarka Line' from Exeter, named after Henry Williamson's novel Tarka the Otter, set in the area.
The town has one of the longest medieval bridges in England still in use, with 16 arches.
Barnstaple is regarded as the principal town of North Devon.
Torre Abbey is Torquay's oldest building, founded as a monastery in 1196.
It now houses a museum with the world's largest collection of Agatha Christie memorabilia, reflecting her links to the town.
Torre station is closer to the abbey than Torquay's main station.
Paignton is part of the 'English Riviera', a stretch of Devon coast known for its mild climate and sandy beaches.
The Paignton and Dartmouth Steam Railway, a heritage line, starts from a station next to the main line terminus.
Paignton Zoo, one of the town's major attractions, sits a short distance inland.
St Austell has been the centre of Cornwall's china clay industry since the mid-18th century.
The distinctive white spoil heaps from clay extraction were once nicknamed the 'Cornish Alps'.
The Eden Project's biomes were built inside one of the area's disused clay pits.
Pendennis Castle was built by Henry VIII around 1540 to defend Falmouth Harbour.
Falmouth has one of the deepest natural harbours in the world.
The Maritime Line branch to Falmouth is one of Cornwall's most scenic short railway lines.
The Towans are a stretch of sand dunes along Hayle's Atlantic coast, popular for walking and wildlife.
Paradise Park in Hayle is home to the World Parrot Trust and breeds rare Cornish choughs for release into the wild.
Hayle was historically an important industrial port for Cornwall's mining industry.
Redruth was at the heart of Cornwall's 18th and 19th century copper and tin mining boom.
The surrounding mining landscape is part of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape World Heritage Site.
Engineer Richard Trevithick, a pioneer of steam locomotion, was born near Redruth.
St Germans has one of the oldest church sites in Cornwall, once the seat of a Cornish bishopric.
The station sits at the head of the St Germans River, a tidal creek off the River Tamar.
The line crosses the Tamar Valley on its way towards Plymouth.
